intro: Rachmaninoff plays the opening of Liszt’s Hungarian Rhapsody No. 2 in C♯ minor, S. 244/2, recorded in 1919, his first year of making gramophone records. This is the first side of Edison Diamond Disc 82169, which holds the slow Lassan with its shifts between major and minor.

sections.label: A · Piano introduction to the Lassan
sections.mNote: A C♯-major chord leads into the minor-key Lassan.

sections.label: B · Softer piano phrases
sections.mNote: A softer continuation after the opening call.

sections.label: C · Piano, stronger phrases
sections.mNote: Stronger phrases follow the quieter passage.

sections.label: D · First side, continued
sections.mNote: Liszt’s rhapsody continues beyond this disc side.

cues.title: Opening chord and Lassan
cues.text: Liszt begins on a C♯-major chord, then moves to C♯ minor for the slow Lassan. The fast Friska comes in the later part of the complete rhapsody.
cues.evidence: The opening major chord, minor-key Lassan and later Friska are described at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hungarian_Rhapsody_No._2. The source identifies this recording as Part I: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Second_Hungarian_Rhapsody.ogg.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Lassan, C♯ major and E major
cues.text: Within the Lassan, Liszt turns repeatedly to C♯ major, the tonic major, and to E major, the relative major. Lighter, capricious passages alternate with the piano’s grave opening.
cues.evidence: The Lassan’s tonic-major and relative-major passages are described at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hungarian_Rhapsody_No._2, under Form.
cues.how: About the passage as a whole.

cues.title: Edison recordings, 1919
cues.text: In 1919 Rachmaninoff began recording for Edison. The contract allowed ten released sides, and he played a Lauter concert grand made in Newark. He asked to approve his performances before release, but Edison issued different takes of the same pieces.
cues.evidence: Rachmaninoff’s first Edison contract, the Lauter piano and the release of multiple takes are described at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sergei_Rachmaninoff_recordings. The selected side’s 1919 date and catalogue number are given at https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Second_Hungarian_Rhapsody.ogg.

cues.title: Rachmaninoff with Stokowski, 1924 and 1929
cues.text: Rachmaninoff later recorded his own Second Piano Concerto with Stokowski and the Philadelphia Orchestra, in 1924 and again in 1929.
cues.evidence: The two recordings of Rachmaninoff’s Second Concerto with Stokowski and the Philadelphia Orchestra are documented at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sergei_Rachmaninoff_recordings.

composer.born: 22 October 1811, Doborján, Kingdom of Hungary (now Raiding, Austria)
composer.epithet: Pianist whose playing drew orchestral sound from the keyboard, and who at the end of his life turned to sparse music at the piano.
facts: Carl Czerny and Antonio Salieri in Vienna; Anton Reicha in Paris
Free masterclasses; founding president of the Budapest music academy, 1875
Piano works and transcriptions; thirteen symphonic poems; symphonies, concertos and sacred music
composer.background:
Writing from Albano in June 1839, Liszt told Princess Cristina Belgiojoso about the concerts he had been giving alone in Rome. No singer came on between his pieces, and no other soloist shared the bill. He played his transcription of the William Tell Overture, fantasies on opera tunes, studies and improvisations. Between numbers he talked to the audience. “The concert is me,” he joked.

His father Adam had begun the piano lessons in Doborján, a German-speaking village in the Kingdom of Hungary, where he worked on an Esterházy estate. Liszt always counted Hungary as his homeland, though the languages he used most easily were German and French. The family went to Vienna in 1822. Carl Czerny, a former pupil of Beethoven, taught him piano, and Antonio Salieri taught him composition. In 1823 the family moved to Paris, where the Conservatoire refused to admit a foreigner. He continued his education with private lessons, including work with Anton Reicha.
